passages.text: The question: Why do human economies, unlike every other order of nature, fail to reach balance (santulan), and what would an economy look like that gives human labour its true value, judged by the usefulness it establishes for human living and for the wider order of nature, rather than by scarcity, accumulation, and price?

A forest, a herd, or a field left to itself settles into a definite balance with its surroundings. Soil feeds plants, plants return to soil, and animals take what their bodies need and then stop. The human body belongs to the same nature. Its requirements for food, shelter, and protection are definite and can be counted, and in principle they could be met and then held in balance like those of any other organism. Human economies nevertheless behave differently. They extract more each generation, accumulate wealth that no one can use, and treat a continuing rise in consumption as the measure of success. Mainstream economics takes this imbalance as its starting point: wants are assumed to be unlimited and means scarce, so economic life becomes the permanent allocation of what is never enough.

Madhyasth Darshan locates the problem elsewhere. The human being is a joint form of a body and jeevan, the conscious unit. The body’s needs are definite; jeevan seeks continuity of happiness, which only understanding fulfils. In delusion, jeevan works through a fraction of its activities and evaluates by pleasure, bodily advantage, and gain. The dissatisfaction of its unexpressed faculties is then taken for a shortage that more sensation and more possession can remove. Because sensory satisfaction is transient and the need it is asked to meet is not material, demand loses its stopping point. Accumulation, above all of money, which alone escapes use and decay, becomes the organising aim of production and exchange.

Shri A. Nagraj set out the darshan’s alternative in Avartansheel Arthshastra, cyclical economics. Body, mind, and wealth are deployed as labour on natural abundance; the objects produced nourish and protect the body and support social life; and these renew the capacity to produce. Exchange rests on the value of labour, need is assessed within the family, production exceeds that need, and the remainder flows into right use.

At the centre of this alternative is a different valuation of human labour. In the darshan, the value (mulya) of anything is its participation in the order of the whole, what its activity fulfils for others (Axiology: Value Theory §1.1). Labour establishes usefulness and beauty in what nature provides, so the true value of labour lies in the usefulness it establishes: in nourishing and protecting the body, in sustaining social life, and, through right use, in the orderliness of family, society, and nature (Axiology §§1.5–1.6). The money economy values labour instead by the price it can command. Labour is bought and sold like any other commodity, the accumulation of currency becomes the measure of a person’s standing, and the producer of useful objects has generally remained poor (AA, pp. 7, 45, 52, 73).

The study reconstructs this account from the treatise and the darshan’s other texts (§§1–3), compares it with economic theory, with Indian and Advaita teaching on desire, and with the sciences of satiation and natural limits (§§4–7), and examines why databases and network connectivity alone cannot establish or run such an economy, how intelligent systems and AI agents paired with individuals, families, and every tier of the ten-stage self-governing order can accelerate the transition and keep the cycle in balance, and what they must leave to people (§8). Its central claim, assessed in the critical review (§9), is that the darshan explains the insatiability that mainstream economics postulates, while it still needs from economics a theory of coordination beyond the village, measurable criteria of need and balance, and an account of money and credit as they actually operate.

passages.heading: 1-why-human-economies-do-not-reach-balance
passages.section: 1. Why human economies do not reach balance
passages.text: 1. Why human economies do not reach balance

passages.heading: 1-why-human-economies-do-not-reach-balance
passages.section: 1. Why human economies do not reach balance
passages.text: 1.1 Balance in every order

passages.heading: 1-why-human-economies-do-not-reach-balance
passages.section: 1. Why human economies do not reach balance
passages.text: Madhyasth Darshan describes nature as four orders: material, biological (plant), animal, and knowledge, the last being the human. Each order maintains its own definite conduct. The material order keeps its conduct through the conformance of its constitution and results; plants reproduce their kind through seed conformance; animals live within the conduct of their species. Every unit of nature except the human exhibits definite conduct, and the human reaches definite conduct only through sanskar, the acceptances formed by understanding (JV, pp. 47–48; AA, pp. 54–55). All traditions other than the human are bound by their own laws and are already orderliness; for the human alone, recognising its own orderliness remains a task (AA, p. 117).

passages.heading: 1-why-human-economies-do-not-reach-balance
passages.section: 1. Why human economies do not reach balance
passages.text: The same account holds that each order is balanced in its existent state. The material order has the innateness of existence, the plant order of existence and growth, and the animal order of existence, growth, and the hope of living, and each is balanced in its existent state. The knowledge order is balanced in its existent state only when it evidences resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, and coexistence (MVD, p. 105). The earth itself is described in these terms. Its seasonal regularity is maintained by definite proportions of minerals and plants, and the coal and mineral oil buried in its interior had a part in making the planet’s heat balance and its later greenery possible (AA, pp. 30, 78–79; KD §3.7, pp. 73–81). Prosperity, on this view, is first a property of the earth, which became rich in itself before any human labour touched it (AA, pp. 77–78).

passages.heading: 1-why-human-economies-do-not-reach-balance
passages.section: 1. Why human economies do not reach balance
passages.text: The conclusion drawn from this account is stark. Whatever unit causes disorder in existence is the deluded human being alone (AA, p. 41). Nature other than human is already complementary to the human; the awakening needed for the human to be complementary to the rest of nature is still awaited (AA, p. 42).

passages.heading: 1-why-human-economies-do-not-reach-balance
passages.section: 1. Why human economies do not reach balance
passages.text: 1.2 The definite needs of the body

passages.heading: 1-why-human-economies-do-not-reach-balance
passages.section: 1. Why human economies do not reach balance
passages.text: The human body is a chemical and physical formation (AA, p. 16). Its needs are of two kinds. Common aspirations are food, shelter, and adornment, together with the objects and equipment needed for health and education; special aspirations are telephony, broadcasting, and transport (AA, pp. 26, 73, 93, 112; JV, p. 113). Both are needs for objects, and objects have definite properties. Grain can be stored for a few years and then rots; a machine left unused rusts; what is produced is for use, and hoarding beyond a point becomes a problem in itself (JV, p. 152). The accumulation of material objects is not feasible, because their use or transformation is inevitable (MVD, p. 183). Even prosperity is a temporal need: work for it is necessary while the body lives, and the need ends with the body (MVD, p. 96). The body also sets the limit of consumption. A person can know more than they can desire, desire more than they can do, and do more than they can consume, and the limit of consuming is the body alone; whatever people produce, they are unable to consume that much (KD, p. 114). A person who understands this produces more and consumes less, with little waste (MVD, p. 282).

passages.heading: 1-why-human-economies-do-not-reach-balance
passages.section: 1. Why human economies do not reach balance
passages.text: The quantities involved can therefore be assessed. For a village of a hundred families, the quantity and quality of food, shelter, and adornment, and the need for medicine, become definite, and on that basis production can be distributed among the families (AA, p. 26). The body’s balance is not an ideal imposed from outside. It is the ordinary condition of a living body whose requirements are met.

passages.heading: 1-why-human-economies-do-not-reach-balance
passages.section: 1. Why human economies do not reach balance
passages.text: 1.3 What an account must explain

passages.heading: 1-why-human-economies-do-not-reach-balance
passages.section: 1. Why human economies do not reach balance
passages.text: If the body’s needs are definite and the rest of nature is balanced, the imbalance of human economies needs an explanation. An adequate account must say why human want becomes insatiable when bodily need does not; how need is to be distinguished from want in practice; how production can be held within the balances on which it depends; how human labour can be given its true value, and exchange made just, when producers differ in skill and circumstance; what evidence would show that such an economy is working; and how a society could move towards it from the present money economy. The darshan’s answer to the first question supplies the ground for the others, so the study begins there.

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: 2.1 Jeevan seeks continuity of happiness

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: Every human being carries out all activities in the hope and expectation of happiness, peace, contentment, and bliss. This expectation is the human’s innateness (dharana), present in every person, and whatever one recognises through the senses is recognised from the expectation of happiness at its root (AA, p. 13). Contentment is accepted by every human being and discontent by none (AA, p. 48).

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: The darshan locates this expectation in jeevan. Jeevan has ten activities, five as powers and five as strengths, borne by its five faculties: mun, with selection and taste; vritti, with analysis and deliberation; chitta, with visualisation and contemplation; buddhi, with resolve and enlightenment; and atma, with authenticity and realisation (AA, p. 50; JV, pp. 72–73). (Here mun names the specific faculty of selection and taste, whereas in the recurring triad “body, mind, and wealth” the word “mind” refers to the jeevan powers as a whole; AA, pp. 59, 62.) The four jeevan values name harmony between adjacent faculties. Happiness is harmony between mun and vritti, peace between vritti and chitta, contentment between chitta and buddhi, and bliss between buddhi and atma (AA, pp. 20–21, 92; JV, p. 137). Happiness in this sense is not a sensation. It is a state of the whole conscious unit, and its continuity depends on the higher faculties having the content of understanding.

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: Deliberation (tulan, in vritti) is the pivot on which this harmony turns. Deliberation in terms of pleasure, health, and profit (priya, hit, labh) can never reach the point of universal agreement between two human beings, since these perspectives are rooted in the body, and no two bodies are the same (JV, pp. 72–73; AA, pp. 58–60). In delusion, justice, dharma, and truth (nyaya, dharma, satya) are interpreted in terms of pleasure, health, and profit, and there is no universal agreement on these aspects either (AA, pp. 18, 59–60). This is the reason there is no balance in human living, including in economics. In awakening, the evaluation perspectives of justice, dharma, and truth are based on understanding and realisation in coexistence, wherein there is universal agreement (AA, pp. 19–20, 58–60; MVD, p. 203). This is the basis of balance in awakened human living, including in economics.

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: 2.2 Four and a half activities and unregulated taste

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: In delusion, only four and a half of the ten activities are effective: selection, taste, analysis, visualisation, and half of deliberation. Taste and selection operate by what is pleasant to the senses; deliberation is confined to the perspectives of pleasure, health, and profit; and the person lives identified with bodily sensation. The remaining activities lack the substance of understanding, and the result is continuous internal conflict within jeevan (JV, pp. 72–73).

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: The treatise draws a consequence from this that bears directly on economics. Selection and tasting form a cycle of their own: after selecting comes tasting, and after tasting the activity of selection arises again. However often the cycle runs, the arising of selection and tasting remains as it was, ready to be done again, because the powers of jeevan are inexhaustible (AA, pp. 17–18). Deliberation in terms of pleasure, health, and profit has been pushed to decisive conclusions in human tradition, while deliberation in terms of justice, dharma, and truth is still under review, its decisive point, form, motion, and purpose not yet settled (AA, p. 18).

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: The awakened alternative is not the suppression of taste. It is its regulation. In awakened jeevan, every tasting is balanced and regulated on the touchstone of deliberation, every deliberation on the touchstone of contemplation, all contemplation on the touchstone of enlightenment, all enlightenment on the touchstone of realisation, and all realisation on the touchstone of coexistence. This chain is the darshan’s formula of self-regulation and balance in every individual (AA, p. 95). Insatiability, on this account, is what selection and tasting become when that chain is missing: an inexhaustible activity with no higher activity to give it measure.

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: 2.3 Transience as a signal, misread as lack

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: Decisions based on sensitivity have temporary validity. Eating feels good, but no one can keep eating; sleeping feels good, but no one can keep sleeping; no sensory activity can be maintained without change. The darshan reads this not as a defect but as a provision:

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: “The transient nature of sensitivity is such a wonderful provision in humans, serving as an alarm, an inspiration, and a direction for their awakening.” — JV, p. 163

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: Whatever process of indulgence a person carries out through the five senses cannot have continuity, and so discontent with it remains in the activity of reflection that follows (AA, p. 48). Temptation towards accumulation and indulgence brings relief for a moment, and in the moments after, fear and suspicion pervade more than relief (AA, p. 33). Pleasure, health, and profit are relative respectively to the senses, the body, and objects; they are the sources of dissatisfaction, whereas justice, dharma, and truth are the sources of satisfaction (AA, pp. 58–59). In the same way, human beings perform labour in the hope of restfulness (vishram), which is achieved in the family and in intellectual resolution; mistaking sensory indulgence for rest leaves the person unfulfilled and weary even after labour ceases (KD, pp. 12–13; AA, p. 23).

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: These passages together give the darshan’s diagnosis of insatiability. The deluded person experiences the discontent that follows every sensory satisfaction and the internal conflict of faculties without content. Lacking understanding of jeevan, the person reads both as a shortage of objects and seeks more of what has just failed to satisfy. The satiation point then moves ahead like a mirage (AA, p. 78). The fulfilment of duties is possible because duties are definite and limited, while the fulfilment of needs pursued as indulgence is impossible because such needs are indefinite and unlimited (MVD, p. 128).

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: The texts also name the lesson that turns this error into economic doctrine. People stray when they are taught that necessities are infinite and means limited, so that necessity can be met only through struggle. That lesson directs attention to accumulation and comfort, neither of which has a point of satisfaction, and leads to the assumption that necessity itself is infinite. Release from it needs clear evidence that each family’s necessity is limited, that the possibility of fulfilling it is greater, that the powers of jeevan are inexhaustible, and that the body’s necessity is limited (KD, p. 115). Profit, which has no point of satisfaction, has no definite measure, and so it cannot be universal (SB, p. 234).

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: Insatiability is thus not a fact about bodily need. It is a category error: a continuous, qualitative need of jeevan pursued through transient, quantitative means. The construction of this synthesis from several connected passages is recorded in the Editorial Notes.

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: 2.4 Accumulation, symbolic value, and artificial scarcity

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: The treatise traces how human provision turned from sharing and barter into profit-obsession. As early communities moved through the forest, stone, and metal ages, they recognised natural materials as resources, shared goods within the family, and bartered between communities to meet real needs (AA, pp. 1–3). Out of fear of natural forces and of one another, people surrendered to the seat of state (rajyapith) for protection in the present life and to the seat of religion (dharmapith) for security in the next (AA, pp. 3–4). When thrones imposed taxes on exchange to fill royal treasuries, traders began adding a margin beyond the tax, initiating what the treatise calls the first stage of profit-obsession (AA, p. 4). Over time, the seat of the market and the seat of leadership displaced royal and religious treasuries as the primary centres of accumulation (AA, pp. 83, 90–91).

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: Profit has always meant giving less and getting more, and prevailing economics has fixed no limit to how much less and how much more (AA, p. 5). The treatise applies this critique to both competing economic systems of the modern era, which it calls unrestrained (aniyantrit, market or capitalist) and regulated (niyantrit, state-controlled or socialist) economics. Neither has determined a fixed point or limit (dhruv) for how much profit or how much accumulation is enough; both evaluate by profit and assume a zero-sum world in which for one unit to gain, another must suffer loss (AA, p. 5). The darshan defines profit against labour: it is seeking more worth than the labour performed, obtaining a higher value in exchange for a lower one (MVD, pp. 57, 66). Profit keeps sinking, through exploitation, into accumulation, indulgence, over-indulgence, and multi-indulgence (AA, p. 7). The treatise concludes that no individual can become prosperous by the method of trade, because accumulation, comfort, and profit have no satiation point; nor can society be formed, contradictions among communities removed, or universal good brought about by that method (AA, pp. 7–8).

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: Accumulation settles on money because money escapes the constraint that governs real goods. Metal became the symbol of objects and paper the symbol of metal, so that economics became the study of a symbol, its accumulating, and objects valued through it (AA, pp. 5–6, 52). Although gold has minimal practical usefulness in daily life, reserves of it are locked in central banks and the International Monetary Fund, while paper currency is also backed by the national stock of every commodity and by central-bank bonds (AA, pp. 44–45). The treatise identifies three allurements that gave paper currency its hold over human society: hundreds of thousands in currency can be carried in a pocket, millions or billions can be stored in a small box, and once all objects and human labour are subjected to currency, accumulating currency becomes the principal basis for recognising a person’s social standing (AA, p. 45). However much paper currency or metal reserve exists, it cannot replace grain for one person or quench one person’s thirst (AA, p. 6; JV, pp. 151–152). The accumulation is only of money, which is symbolic value (MVD, p. 182). Changes in price over decades are changes in the symbol alone; rice, gold, and cement carry the same usefulness as before (AA, pp. 52–53). The practice of collecting interest and the share market multiply claims in symbolic currency further still (AA, p. 52).

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: Subjecting society to currency gave rise to what the treatise classifies as seven kinds of trade: five forms of trade in persons (trading in strength by hiring the strong, in learning by hiring the educated, in knowledge by selling understanding, which the treatise calls the most wicked trade, in position or office, and in beauty), together with trade in produced objects and trade in industrial technology, which buys salaried scholars and technicians to secure monopolies (AA, pp. 45–46). As the centres of accumulation shifted from royal and religious treasuries to middlemen and traders, the highest accumulators in the second half of the twentieth century came to include film and stage performers and figures of commercialised beauty alongside merchants and financiers (AA, pp. 90–91).

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: Two further consequences follow. Artificial scarcity becomes a principal technique for gaining profit: where currency is concentrated, objects are held back from the motion by which they would become accessible to all (AA, pp. 5–6, 52). And because accumulation has no satiation point, it cannot be accessible to all, since the earth is limited (AA, p. 52). Those who remain engaged in production are unable to accumulate, while those who accumulate become slack in production, and the producer of objects has generally remained poor (AA, pp. 7, 75). The widening distance between producer and consumer, filled by profit, is one of the two discords the treatise finds in present production; pollution is the other (AA, p. 106).

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: The darshan names the error in terms of evaluation. Delusion means taking a thing to be more than, less than, or other than what it is (AA, p. 17). Over-evaluation of symbolic currency, under-evaluation of usefulness value, mis-evaluation of the human being as a kind of animal, and under-evaluation of naturalness, the forests, minerals, and earth on which all provision depends, are its economic forms (AA, p. 53).

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: 2.5 The consequence in the earth

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: The same evaluation produces the ecological crisis. Here the treatise draws a sharp line between production and extraction. Humans do not produce mineral oil, coal, or ores; nature placed them in the strata of the earth before human beings existed, as part of the planet’s own balance. Tearing open the earth to remove them is extraction and seizure, not production, and is defended only by the circular excuse of preserving the livelihoods tied to that extraction (AA, p. 78). Coal and mineral oil needed to remain in the earth for its balance; extracting and burning them produced pollution, rising heat, a damaged protective layer in the upper atmosphere, and rising seas (AA, pp. 30–31). Chemical fertilisers increased quantity while the concentration of nutrition in grain declined and soils were driven towards excess acidity or alkalinity (AA, p. 70). Breeding produced larger grains and flowers whose basic nutritive content stayed the same (AA, pp. 53, 55–56). Mechanised and input-dependent agriculture replaced autonomy with dependence in seed, manure, ploughing, and threshing (AA, p. 71). Pollution policy, in the treatise’s assessment, does not ask how to stop pollution but how much of it people can live in (AA, p. 74).

passages.heading: 2-the-joint-form-and-the-source-of-insatiability
passages.section: 2. The joint form and the source of insatiability
passages.text: The whole form of exploitation is the exploitation of the earth, and the human being is both exploited and exploiter (AA, p. 82). The only production the treatise names as opposed in itself to a coexistential economy is the manufacture of war materials; machine production as such is not contrary to economics (AA, p. 47). The objection is to the purpose and the evaluation that direct production, not to technique.

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: 3. Cyclical economics

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: 3.1 Resources as body, mind, and wealth

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Cyclical economics is the right use, security, and prosperity of resources (artha) in the form of body, mind, and wealth (AA, p. 25). The mind is an inseparable activity of jeevan. When hope, thought, desire, and resolve act by a realisation-based method, the mind works through the body, applying labour with skill and proficiency to natural abundance. In this process, the powers of jeevan project outward (paravartan) through the cognitive and work organs as dexterity (hastalaghav) to establish usefulness value and aesthetic value in natural materials, and reflect inward (pratyavartan) as the strengthening of jeevan’s own faculties (AA, pp. 18–19, 48–50). The objects produced carry usefulness value and aesthetic value, and these objects are wealth (dhan); wealth is only the produced object, not money (AA, pp. 25, 105). The right use of the body is evidenced when the mind uses it consistently with realisation, enlightenment, contemplation, and deliberation (AA, p. 25).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: This changes what counts as capital. All production is the outcome of human labour applied to natural abundance, so the primary wealth is the labour power inherent in human beings, and this primary capital is always the human being’s own (AA, p. 73). The means of a human being are only body, mind, and wealth (MVD, p. 243). Earning wealth is the definite measure of usefulness and aesthetic value realised from natural abundance through the planned deployment of human labour (MVD, p. 56). Because the powers of jeevan are inexhaustible, every human being has the capacity to produce more than immediate necessity, and this is the foundational principle of human prosperity (SB, p. 268). Public dialogue on the economy can therefore begin from the recognition that human labour is the primary capital (JVD, p. 215). Economics that treats money as the primary resource has studied the symbol rather than the thing (JV, pp. 151–152). Resources must include body, mind, and wealth together; economics cannot exist if any one of these is left out (JV, p. 151).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: 3.2 What cyclicality means

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: The treatise gives cyclicality a wide sense before it gives it an economic one. Complementarity itself is the meaning of cyclicality, and cyclicality is mutual sustenance: particles sustain one another as atoms, atoms as molecules, molecules as formations, and the orders of nature as one another’s support (AA, p. 42). It can be seen at many scales. Seed becomes tree and tree becomes seed; bodies form according to species and species traditions continue through bodies; knowing and believing ground recognising and fulfilling, and these return to knowing and believing; relationship grounds value, value grounds evaluation, and evaluation returns to relationship. The individual’s complementarity is linked into the family and the family’s into the individual, and the same holds between family and village. Production through the utilisation of labour, the valuation of products by the value of labour, and exchange on that basis together form a cycle, and so do the four orders, each complementary to the others (AA, p. 15). Water evaporates, gathers as cloud, falls as rain, and runs back to the sea; plants decompose and make the earth fertile for further plants (AA, pp. 34–35; MVD, p. 152).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: The common structure is a movement that starts from any point, passes through complementary activity towards the fulfilment of a purpose, and returns to its starting point with that purpose fulfilled, so that the movement can continue (AA, p. 15). The treatise’s own definition of this structure is a compressed sentence whose Hindi admits more than one parsing; the reading adopted here is recorded in the Editorial Notes. Two features of it matter for economics. A cycle returns: whatever is drawn out is restored to the conditions of the next round. And a cycle is purposive: it is linked in the sense of prosperity, so its return is the fulfilment of a goal, not mere repetition.

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: 3.3 The provision cycle

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Applied to provision, the cycle has a definite sequence. A need for production arises; a mentality fitted to that need, endowed with skill, proficiency, and scholarliness, forms; through a healthy body, labour establishes usefulness value and aesthetic value in objects drawn from natural abundance; the objects are rightly used according to their usefulness; the need is supplied; and the remainder is exchanged (AA, p. 106). The Jeevan Vidya lectures state the same cycle as a renewal of capacity:

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: “We deploy our resources in the form of body, mind, and wealth on natural abundance for production, and the produced goods become the basis of nourishment and protection of our body and social participation. We again become capable of producing on the basis of this social participation, nourishment, and protection. In this way, it is cyclical.” — JV, p. 154

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: The cycle runs through the joint form itself. The mind operates the body; mind and body together manifest object values; and object values are useful to the body and satisfying to jeevan (AA, p. 26). Earth, air, water, forest, and minerals are the sites where labour is utilised (AA, p. 26). Tools and other means made by one generation serve the next, so that means accumulate across generations in a form that remains in use: each generation can offer the next means in excess of need, the means of production increase, and the time required decreases (AA, pp. 106, 118). The cycle grows richer without growing larger in consumption.

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: 3.4 Need, the family, and prosperity

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: The cycle closes only where need is definite, and the darshan locates that definiteness in the family. A family is a limited number of autonomous people, at least ten, living together with justice: recognising their relationships, fulfilling the values in them, evaluating, and reaching mutual satisfaction, and complementary to one another in the family’s production (AA, pp. 14, 26, 65, 72). The treatise states that the cyclical economy becomes meaningful only after balance is achieved in human relationships: where relationships are balanced, objects are used in the service of those relationships, free of profit and loss (AA, p. 21). Needs are ascertained at the level of the family, not the individual (JV, p. 153; AA, p. 9), and they are assessed by the family itself rather than rationed from above. This definiteness is not austere uniformity: it encompasses both common aspirations (food, shelter, adornment, health, and education) and special aspirations (telephony, broadcasting, and transport), together with aesthetic value and regulated taste (AA, pp. 95, 112). In a humane family, needs become limited because use, right use, and purposeful use become definite, and production in excess of need is therefore possible in every family (AA, p. 26). Production beyond necessity is already evident before awakening, since relatively few people produce what many more use; in a wise family, two to four members may produce beyond the family’s whole necessity (KD, p. 115). For a person who understands jeevan, all needs are useful only in the nourishment and protection of the body and in social participation, so needs appear limited, while the labour power for meeting them, being the inexhaustible power of jeevan, gives confidence in production in excess of need (AA, p. 114).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Prosperity follows directly. The lack of the sentiment of lacking is prosperity, and production in excess of needs is prosperity (MVD, p. 71). Its basis is the sum of objects produced in excess of need, together with their right use and security (AA, p. 113). Prosperity cannot be private. For one family to be prosperous, more than one family must be; both the imagining of prosperity alone and the imagining of prosperity through accumulation prove to be delusion (AA, pp. 62–63). The person who can sustain this is the autonomous human: trusting in oneself, respecting excellence, balanced in talent and personality, social in behaviour, and self-reliant in occupation (AA, pp. 65, 71–72). Because the household is a small, mutually visible community of ten persons in which work is organised so as to remain restful (vishram) rather than exhausting (KD, pp. 12–13; AA, pp. 14, 119–120), and because social honour and eligibility to represent the family in the self-governing councils rest on living with resolution and producing in excess of need (AA, pp. 125–126; MVD, p. 265), sharing according to need within the family does not invite the anonymous shirking that afflicts impersonal wage or welfare systems (AA, pp. 75–76).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: 3.5 Use, right use, and purposeful use

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Use, right use, and purposeful use name three levels at which resources serve human purposes. Usefulness is the utilisation of body, mind, and wealth in the nourishment and protection of the body and in social participation. Right use is their utilisation in orderliness and in the motion of undivided society. Purposeful use is their utilisation in evidencing, from generation to generation, knowledge of coexistence, of jeevan, and of humane conduct (AA, pp. 72, 94). The darshan’s glossary states the same levels in terms of participation: use is the deployment of means for production and service, right use is their utilisation within the family-based self-governing order, and purposeful use is their utilisation, upon awakening, towards undivided society and universal orderliness (MVD, p. 56). Body, mind, and wealth are indivisible in all three, because no object can be used without body and mind (AA, p. 94). The treatise pairs usefulness with justice, right use with resolution, and purposeful use with authenticity (AA, p. 116). In terms of scale, production is used within the family, rightly used in society, and put to purpose in the universal order (KD, p. 116). Among the human goals, prosperity is realised through the right use and security of object values, fearlessness through established and civic values, and resolution through human and jeevan values (AA, p. 68).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Values are ordered by what they serve across a thirty-value hierarchy (Axiology: Value Theory §1.6). In offering and surrender, the two object values (usefulness value and aesthetic value) are dedicated to the nine civic or expressed values, the nine civic values to the nine established values of relationship (such as trust, respect, and affection), the nine established values to the six human values (steadfastness, courage, generosity, kindness, grace, and compassion), and the six human values to the four jeevan values, which are happiness, peace, contentment, and bliss (AA, pp. 20–24, 92). The right use of resources is itself cyclicality, and the earth’s endowment is rightly used by the method of balance (AA, p. 91). Karm Darshan ranks the pursuit of wealth in seven steps against the classical aims of life: wealth placed in the service of liberation, dharma, or the fulfilment of desire is ranked high, those three purposes placed in the service of wealth are ranked low, and wealth sought for its own sake falls in between (KD, p. 4). Non-accumulation means earning for expenditure, and its righteous expenditure is mandatory (MVD, p. 150). Those who take no part in production lack awakening regarding use and right use (AA, p. 75).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: 3.6 Value, labour, and exchange

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Value in Madhyasth Darshan is not price. The value of a unit is its essentiality, its participation in the orderliness of the whole: what its activity fulfils in relation to others. For produced things this participation is usefulness, what food, shelter, a tool, or a vehicle fulfils in nourishing and protecting the body and in social participation, and aesthetic value adds convenience to usefulness. As §3.5 showed, usefulness serves need, and need serves relationships, humane character, and finally the harmonies of jeevan (Axiology: Value Theory §§1.1, 1.5–1.6; AA, p. 92). Human labour is the activity that establishes usefulness and beauty upon natural abundance, and the primary wealth of any economy is this labour power, which is always the human being’s own (AA, p. 73). To give labour its true value is to value it by the usefulness it establishes in this larger sense, not by the currency it can command.

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Production is the usefulness value and aesthetic value established through labour on natural abundance, in the sense of prosperity (AA, p. 68). It is also described as the human establishment of usefulness and beauty upon nature other than human, and as a qualitative change in body, mind, and natural abundance in the direction of usefulness (AA, p. 116). The value of an object is determined in a chain: labour-based object, object-based usefulness, usefulness-based valuation (AA, p. 49). Evaluation can be made only of labour, not of symbolic objects (AA, p. 112).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Labour in the darshan is not physical exertion alone; it is the joint deployment of mind (manas, the powers of jeevan) and body together with means upon natural abundance, requiring skill (kushalata), a mind full of proficiency (nipunata), and scholarliness (panditya) (AA, pp. 26, 59, 62, 118–119). The treatise proposes a practical method of valuing this labour. Wheat sown in a village under various circumstances yields various quantities; the midpoint of those quantities gives a common value for the labour of producing wheat. Once one object of common aspiration has been valued in this way, every product of the village can be valued similarly, and the valuation can be consolidated within the village (AA, p. 66). Each person’s pace of work (karya-gati) in an activity, in ploughing, breaking stone, building a house, weaving, or making machines, differs by activity and is the basis of measurement. A product of measured quantity and quality made in a definite time, through a definite technical mentality and dexterity, counts as one unit of labour and can be exchanged for labour equal to it (AA, p. 119). The production and exchange-reserve committees jointly determine the quantity, quality, and labour values of village products, and the exchange committee evaluates labour through the fivefold combination of skill, proficiency, speed of work, time, and means, remaining alert so that neither unnecessary profit nor unbearable loss occurs (AA, pp. 143, 145). Valuing labour by this fivefold combination measures the useful output established with competent skill and tools, rather than rewarding slowness or counting raw hours of physical toil. Because tools and means accumulate across generations, the labour required per unit of output decreases over time, and the unit value of labour in objects is revised downward accordingly (AA, pp. 118, 145).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: This valuation establishes a satiation point within exchange itself. Production is the remuneration of labour, and after exchange the remuneration remains just as much as was produced. This is the satiation point of exchange: in the utilisation of labour there is neither profit nor loss, only more or less production as a matter of work practice (AA, p. 76). The treatise extends the point to existence as a whole. Neither development in the atom, nor the transition to jeevan, nor the formation and decomposition of physical and chemical substances shows any sign of profit and loss; what is seen throughout is coexistence and prosperity (AA, pp. 77–78).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Differences of skill do not have to be weighed inside the family. The treatise asks explicitly whether dexterity of hand, skill, proficiency, and scholarliness can be the same in every person, and answers that within a family of ten members some days one person is more complementary in production and some days less; the family’s goal is the product, not more or less individual labour (AA, pp. 119–120). Valuation by labour is needed between families and villages, where exchange takes place. Usefulness value itself is constant: a kilogram of sesame has always had the same usefulness, whatever its monetary valuation (JV, pp. 136–137).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: 3.7 Righteous wealth, generosity, and care

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: The ethics of the economy are stated in terms of character. Humane character consists of righteous wealth, marital faithfulness, and kindness in work and behaviour (AA, p. 54). Righteous wealth (svadhan) is wealth received as the remuneration of one’s own labour, as a gift, or as an award (puraskar) for a special display of art, technique, or scholarship; whoever holds it, it is the result of someone’s labour on natural abundance (AA, p. 140; AVD, p. 170). Its opposite, ill-gotten wealth, is wealth obtained through exploitation and hypocrisy, and the darshan counts it, with adultery and hurting others, as crime (MVD, pp. 59, 263). Moral responsibility across economic life extends to three modes of participation across body, speech, and mind: doing an act oneself (krit), commissioning another to do it (karit), and consenting to or endorsing it (anumodit) (KD, pp. 1–2, 117; SB, pp. 207, 258). Financing or knowingly profiting from exploitation or ecological harm therefore carries the same accountability as direct action. The same distinction separates lawful from unlawful use of nature. Spending minerals and forests in proportion to their regeneration and maintaining circularity in natural abundance are lawful; spending beyond regeneration and exploiting non-renewable materials are not (MVD, p. 263).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: The treatise connects these economic orientations to five kinds of human living within the knowledge order (AA, p. 101). Before awakening, the animalistic human (pashu manav) lives in narrow selfishness and indulgence, and the demonic human (rakshas manav) in cruel selfishness and over-indulgence. Upon awakening, the humane human (manav) evidences resolution and prosperity by producing in excess of need and practising right use; the deific human (dev manav) evidences benevolence by dedicating body, mind, and wealth to the awakening and orderliness of others; and the divine human (divya manav) evidences compassion in unbroken universality (AA, pp. 23–24, 101). Awakening replaces interest-based (ruchimulak) consumption, driven by fluctuating sensory preferences, with value-based (mulyamulak) and goal-based (lakshyamulak) living, in which education fosters more production and less consumption (AA, pp. 101–102, 132).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: The darshan does not ask people to renounce wealth. While animals are bound by four instincts (food, sleep, fear, and reproduction), humans act with three motives (eshana): the desire for progeny (putreshana), for wealth (vitteshana), and for reputation or public welfare (lokeshana) (MVD, p. 318). In an awakened person attraction takes the form of pursuing prosperity with righteous motives (MVD, pp. 59, 137). Among the three, the motive for public welfare is the highest, because through it a person extends participation from the family to undivided society and universal orderliness (MVD, p. 320). People, wealth, and reputation are assets of the family and of the undivided society rather than of the individual (MVD, p. 221), and wealth finds its success and satisfaction through generosity (MVD, pp. 211, 254). Generosity is the happy offering of body, mind, and wealth, according to need, for the awakening, bodily health, and prosperity of others, and the treatise reads every kind of cyclicality as a sign of it (MVD, p. 339; AA, p. 22).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Within the family, goods are shared and allotted; between families and communities they are exchanged (AA, p. 1). Those who cannot produce are provided for through kindness, which includes making an object available where there is receptivity for it but no object. The works of kindness the treatise lists include helping people who are helpless, in distress, afflicted by disease, or struck by natural calamity (AA, pp. 23–24, 140). Guardians who feed their child first and eat what is left already show the human tendency to let others live and then live oneself (AA, p. 102), and parents nurture and protect their children and make them capable of production (MVD, p. 340). Once a family is resolved and prosperous, the question of where its further production should go is answered by the propensity of benevolence that then arises (KD, p. 116). How, then, do individuals engaged in service (seva) obtain the physical objects that fulfil their needs when they do not themselves bring a new material commodity to exchange? The texts treat agriculture and industry as the two primary forms of production and classify all other vocations as dependent on or complementary to them (MVD, p. 267), while distinguishing two forms of service: benevolence-focused service (upkar-pradhan seva), done for the satisfaction of benevolence without material return, and remuneration-focused service (pratiphal-pradhan seva), done for remuneration (parishramik), which counts as righteous wealth (svadhan) (MVD, pp. 72, 263; AA, p. 140). Those performing benevolence-focused service, including household care, child and elder support, teaching, part-time work on the five village committees (AA, p. 127), and full-time representation in the ten-tier council order (lok-pratinidhi), live within a ten-member family where two to four members already produce beyond the whole household’s needs; Karm Darshan states explicitly that all objects needed for a representative’s bodily nourishment, protection, and societal motion remain provided by their prosperous family (KD, pp. 115–117; AA, pp. 119–120). Conversely, for dedicated village services listed as the ninth branch of the village production system, such as repairing bicycles, radios, televisions, and agricultural or industrial machines, washing clothes, barbering, or staffing the exchange-reserve (AA, pp. 133, 136, 138), the service preserves or restores the usefulness of produced goods and village operations; the village family council fixes the remuneration for the service (AA, p. 136), and because every resident holds an account in the village’s autonomous cooperative exchange-reserve (AA, pp. 137–138), that remuneration credits their account so they can draw food, clothing, and other needed objects from the reserve at labour value. Because every villager is also trained in more than one occupation (AA, p. 131) and belongs to a ten-member family, service work complements household production rather than creating a landless service class.

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: 3.8 Production within the balance of nature

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: The provision cycle is nested within the cycles of nature, and its production must keep them intact. Natural assets, minerals and vegetation, are to be used in proportion to their production, in the sense of balance; their production is not to be obstructed; and human beings are to become helpful in it. Without keeping nature prosperous, the human being cannot be prosperous (AA, pp. 142, 146; KD, p. 7). The state policy of the darshan names production security as maintained “through the principle of maintaining nature’s balance”, and economic security through producing more than the needs of the family by way of circularity (MVD, p. 264).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: The treatise is specific about energy. Mineral oil, coal, and radioactive fuels are the most harmful sources; cyclical sources, the force of flowing water, falling water, wind, solar heat, and gas from dung and refuse, are pollution-free (AA, pp. 31–32, 106–107; JV, pp. 115–116). Vegetable oil from roadside oil-bearing trees forms a closed cycle: tree, seed, oil, smoke, the smoke taken up as food by trees, and seed again (AA, p. 32). Agriculture is to keep animal husbandry, compost, and dung gas together, so that the village’s own manure restores fertility and soil degradation is halted (AA, pp. 134–135). The human-made environment must be planned with attention to the interventions made upon nature, the utilisations of labour, their returns, and their usefulness, right use, and purposeful use (AA, p. 114). Determining the land of each village and district also determines how many villages can live there with prosperity (AA, p. 92).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: 3.9 Skill, knowledge, and dissemination

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Since labour is the primary capital, the formation of skill is central to the economy. Education is to make skill, proficiency, and scholarliness accessible to every person, so that each becomes competent in production (AA, p. 113). The darshan’s state policy calls for skills to be made commonly accessible together with understanding, for resources to be allotted to people with skill, and for research and development directed towards food, shelter, adornment, telecommunication, and transport (MVD, pp. 267–268). In the village, the education committee works with the production and exchange-reserve committees to decide who should be trained in which occupation, in view of the village’s present and future needs, and ensures that villagers become proficient in more than one occupation so that seasonal and technical shifts do not leave anyone idle (AA, p. 131). Teachers and scholars carry technical knowledge to ordinary people as a work of benevolence (AA, p. 29). Education that imparts only vocational knowledge serves material prosperity alone (MVD, p. 307); humane education adds the understanding that keeps production within its purposes.

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Knowledge is not to be enclosed. Farmers handed on their seeds and methods without concealment, and research and its dissemination are inseparable. Monopolies over seed and what modern law calls intellectual property rights obstruct that relation, turning discoveries meant for universal welfare into instruments of commercial exploitation; since the powers of jeevan cannot be deposited in any bank or reserve, intellectual reservation is meaningless (AA, pp. 56–58; JV, pp. 88–89). What one human being can understand, every human being can understand, and what one attains, all can attain (AA, p. 107). Trading in knowledge, like trading in human labour and in religion, is among the forms of profit the texts reject (AA, p. 45; AVD, p. 53).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Rejecting patent monopolies does not mean leaving invention unrecognised or unmotivated. Under the treatise’s provisions for the security of production, whenever a person or group evidences a special originality (maulikta) in production, such as an original tool, procedure, method, design, or medicinal or craft discovery not previously in the tradition, the justice-security committee, working with the production, health-restraint, and education committees, formally secures its drawings, formulas, and procedures in writing for the tradition and arranges prizes and awards (puraskar), which constitute righteous wealth (svadhan) (AA, pp. 140, 144). Four factors motivate technical invention in the absence of commercial monopolies. First, because household needs are definite, disseminating a labour-saving tool lowers the unit labour value of goods and directly reduces the working hours required from every family, including the inventor’s own (AA, pp. 118, 145). Second, once basic quantities are met, the attention of jeevan turns naturally towards quality and creative doership (kartritva) (AA, pp. 116, 118). Third, original contributions earn public honour (lokeshana, the highest of the three human motives) together with formal awards (MVD, pp. 318, 320; AA, pp. 140, 144). Fourth, sharing a discovery so that other families can produce with less strain directly fulfils benevolence (upkar) (AA, pp. 29, 101).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: 3.10 Machines, automation, and the participation of every person

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Machine production is not contrary to economics (AA, p. 47). Technique multiplies the speed of whatever humans do. Until people can live as members of society and of an orderly system, that multiplication increases the speed of problems and the number of crimes; only with such understanding do machines become available to every family as prosperity (SB, p. 267). The treatise names two drives that have kept technique from serving this purpose: the preoccupation with making all production automatic, and the centralisation of industry. Both rest on capital investment and on buying labour power. Automatic production has reduced the number of people engaged in production, so that of two equally educated people one finds work and the other feels useless (AA, p. 107). A working mindset has given way to a managing mindset, one reason why no balance has yet been reached in the evaluation of remuneration for the objects of common and special aspiration (JVD, p. 35). Salaried work tends to slacken once employment is secure, and those most adept in production present themselves at home as entitled to comfort and rule (AA, pp. 75–76).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Against this, every person is to be engaged in production according to capacity, receptivity, and ability (MVD, p. 265; AA, p. 127). When every member of every family takes part in production, poverty, deprivation, and the trap of accumulation and comfort are left behind together (JVD, p. 216). The exchange-reserve works with the education committee to replace the salaried mentality with a production mentality, and helps traders turn from hoarding to production (AA, p. 137). Large industry keeps its place at the higher tiers of the order, while most technology stays within small industry (AA, pp. 29–30, 115). Means rightly used let each generation pass on more means in excess of need, so that the means of production increase and the time required decreases (AA, p. 118). The darshan’s criterion for technique is therefore twofold: it should increase the usefulness that labour establishes and reduce the time it takes, and it should keep every person a participant in production rather than displacing people from it.

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: 3.11 The economy within the five dimensions of orderliness

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Economics in isolation has no definition or standing (AA, p. 117). Cyclical economics is one integral part of self-governance, alongside sociology, the science of the constitution, psychology, and the science of production (AA, pp. 63, 110). Self-governance means accessibility to justice, to production, and to exchange, sustained by education-sanskar and health-restraint (AA, p. 63). The treatise grounds this order in the progression from the autonomous human (swayatt manav) to the family human (parivar manav) and the orderliness human (vyavastha manav), through three inseparable qualities: authority (adhikar, the strength of understanding and realisation), identity (swatva, evidencing that strength in living), and independence (swatantrata, unconstrained participation in family and universal orderliness) (AA, pp. 104–105). It contrasts this family-based order with power-centric rule (whether monarchy, majority-mandate party democracy, or power-centric village councils, panchayats), which seeks to enforce order through fear and inducement, and with international relief that measures human rights in money rather than awakening (AA, pp. 82–84). The five dimensions of orderliness are depicted as a circle joined to a pentagon: education-sanskar to understanding, health-restraint to expression consistent with science and wisdom, justice-security to honesty, production to prosperity, and exchange-reserve to balance (AA, p. 112). How Undivided Society Is Established §5.4 describes how these dimensions constrain one another.

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: The village of about a hundred families is the first unit of this order. Ten families form a family cluster, ten clusters a village council, and so on through ten tiers to a world family council, each council nominating five committees for the five dimensions (AA, pp. 27–28, 125–127). Because representatives at each tier are selected by consensus from the tier below rather than through adversarial campaigning, election expenditure drops to zero (AA, p. 110). Committee members serve on a part-time basis while continuing their own production, so governance does not create a non-producing political class (AA, p. 127). Production scale rises with the tier: cottage industry within the village, small industry at the village cluster, medium industry at the district, medium and large industry at the province, and large industry at the region, continent, and world, where the world council’s committees maintain balance across the whole (AA, pp. 29–30, 115). Within the village, the production committee coordinates nine branches of work: agriculture, goatery and dairy (cow-rearing), clothing, shelter construction, food processing, repair and maintenance, forest resources, clean energy, and local manufacture (AA, pp. 133–136). The exchange-reserve is staffed by at least three trained persons who maintain accounts of production, consumption, and exchange (AA, p. 138). Every village is to be autonomous in the objects of common aspiration, while a shortfall in a few items is met reciprocally within ten or a hundred villages and complex goods for special aspirations (transport, telecommunications, broadcasting, and heavy equipment) are produced by medium and large industries at the higher tiers (AA, pp. 29–30, 72, 115). Risk from crop failure or natural calamity, and upfront provisioning for shared facilities, are met without commercial insurance or interest-bearing capital markets through three buffers: family and village surpluses held in the exchange-reserve, reciprocal deficit coverage and works of kindness across the ten-village and hundred-village tiers (AA, pp. 23–24, 72, 140), and common-facility funds administered by the councils (AA, pp. 128, 137–138). Common aspirations are assessed through local survey and special aspirations through local acceptability (AA, p. 112). Justice is assessed in four dimensions: in character, in behaviour, in production, and in exchange (AA, pp. 140–143).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: 3.12 The three policies and exchange between regions

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: The darshan names three policies for the resources of body, mind, and wealth. Their protection is the concern of state policy (raj-neeti), their right use of moral policy (dharm-neeti), and production beyond the family’s needs of economic policy (arth-neeti) (KD, p. 67; MVD, pp. 233, 239). Moral policy is primary and permanent, whereas state policy is subordinate to it and transitions from protective regulation into self-governing orderliness as understanding spreads (KD, p. 14; MVD, p. 239). The darshan’s state policy sets out six securities: national security through coexistence, economic security through producing more than the family’s needs by way of circularity, production security through maintaining nature’s balance, exchange security through the utilisation and exchange of labour, education security through knowledge of coexistence, and ethical security through the right use and security of body, mind, and wealth (MVD, pp. 264, 271).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: These provisions bear directly on the value of human labour. Economic security calls for every person to be enabled to work productively according to capacity, receptivity, and ability, for respect and honour to be conferred on that basis, for the disparity between rich and poor to end through resolution and prosperity in every family, and for righteous wealth to be established through higher production and lower consumption. Production security names agriculture and industry as the two primary forms of production (with all other vocations dependent on or complementary to them), calls for a policy that prevents the exploitation of the fruits of labour, and measures the success of the production system by every family producing more than its needs and achieving prosperity (MVD, pp. 259, 265–268). Exchange security defines exchange as making produced goods available to consumers on the basis of the evaluation of human labour, free of profit and loss (MVD, pp. 265–268). Exchange between nations is likewise to be free of profit and loss and based on object value and labour value (MVD, p. 268). Karm Darshan adds that while karma-governed exchange is free of gain and loss, exchange is freed from class sentiment (varg-bhavna) only when grounded in the humane rule-trio of intellectual, social, and natural laws (KD, pp. 15, 35, 42). Under present arrangements, countries holding large foreign exchange reserves are able to exploit others (JVD, p. 32).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: 3.13 The path of transition

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: The treatise does not assume that the money economy disappears at once. Its plan for a village begins with a detailed survey: population, education, occupations, land, water, crops, livestock, crafts, shops, storage, health, and the state of justice in production and in exchange (AA, pp. 122–125). The village’s exchange is then conducted through an autonomous cooperative exchange-reserve working without profit and loss. Members hold accounts, sell to the reserve what they produce in excess of need, and buy what they need. In the first period, values follow the nearby market rate less the cost of transport; any incidental gain from trading with outside markets goes to the village’s common facilities; members without funds receive interest-free loans repaid in produce; and a nationalised cooperative bank stands as guarantor until the reserve can return its capital (AA, pp. 136–138).

passages.heading: 3-cyclical-economics
passages.text: Justice in exchange is reached in three stages. First, the value of labour is evaluated through the prevailing currency, using wholesale rates. Second, the currency itself is evaluated on the basis of labour. Third, object values are evaluated on the value of labour alone, through usefulness and aesthetic value, and exchange proceeds free of profit, loss, and accumulation (AA, pp. 142–143). The Jeevan Vidya lectures add that the wish for a cyclical economy is present even in people living within a profit-obsessed system, and that producing in excess of need by one’s own labour is open to anyone now; Nagraj records that he lived with prosperity through his own production within the prevailing currency-based system (JV, pp. 153–154; AVD, p. 52). The public dialogue proposed for families puts the choice plainly: whether to live with autonomy, resolution, and prosperity or in dependency and accumulation, and whether the economy is to be driven by profit and symbolic currency or by exchange on the value of labour (JVD, pp. 217–218). Each committee’s work is evaluated against stated criteria. Production is evaluated by total output, speed, quality, productivity, skill, access to raw materials, and pollution-free technical improvement; exchange by its ease, its freedom from profit and loss, its cleanness, its measurement, and its management of means (AA, pp. 146–148).

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: 4.1 Aristotle: household management and unlimited acquisition

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: Aristotle distinguished the art of household management, which acquires what is needed for living well, from the art of wealth-getting through exchange for gain. The first has a limit set by the needs of the household and the city; the second has no limit to its end, because it pursues money as such. He judged retail trade for gain contrary to nature and usury the most unnatural mode of acquisition, since it makes money breed money (Aristotle, Politics I.8–10; SEP-AP). The parallel with the darshan’s closure condition is close. Natural wealth has a measure because it serves use, and acquisition becomes limitless when it attaches to the symbol of wealth.

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: 4.2 Classical political economy, differential rent, and the stationary state

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: The classical economists located the source of wealth in labour and expected growth eventually to give way to a stationary state of capital and population. David Ricardo showed that when land or mines differ in natural fertility and location, equal quantities of labour yield unequal quantities of produce; if goods exchange at a common value set by less fertile land, producers on more fertile land capture a differential rent that arises from nature’s endowment rather than additional human effort (Ricardo 1817). Any system that values products by a midpoint or average of labour across varying soils and regions must account for such differential endowments (§§8.3, 9.1). John Stuart Mill declined to regard the prospect of a stationary state with the aversion of his predecessors. A stationary condition of capital and population, he argued, implies no stationary state of human improvement, and might leave more room for culture, moral progress, and the preservation of nature than a society absorbed in getting on (Mill, Principles IV.6). Mill’s stationary state halts accumulation by choice, for the sake of a better life; it lacks the darshan’s account of why accumulation outruns need in the first place.

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: 4.3 Marx: use, accumulation, and the value of labour

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: Marx contrasted the circuit of simple commodity circulation, in which a commodity is sold for money in order to buy another commodity for use, with the circuit of capital, in which money buys commodities in order to be sold for more money. The first ends in consumption and so has a natural limit; the second begins and ends with money, and its movement is therefore limitless (Marx, Capital I, ch. 4). He grounded value in socially necessary labour time, the labour required under prevailing average conditions of skill and technique, and treated skilled labour as compound or multiplied simple labour because prior labour went into forming the worker’s skill (Marx, Capital I, ch. 1). Under capitalism, an innovator who introduces a labour-saving tool captures temporary extra surplus value until the technique spreads and lowers the socially necessary labour time of the product. In his Critique of the Gotha Programme, Marx distinguished two sequential phases of post-capitalist distribution: a first phase in which producers receive individual labour-time certificates after deductions for common funds and draw from the social stock goods of equal labour value, and a higher phase in which, after the productive forces and all-round human development have grown, society distributes from each according to ability to each according to need. Because workers differ in skill, strength, and family responsibilities, Marx noted that first-stage labour certificates still operate under an unequal “bourgeois right”, yielding unequal individual consumption claims until the higher phase is reached (Marx, Gotha Programme).

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: The darshan shares much of Marx’s diagnosis of capital: profit as giving less and taking more, labour as the source of all product, and the endlessness of accumulation in money. Where Marx separated need-based distribution and equal labour-value exchange into two historical stages and tied first-stage claims to the individual worker’s labour certificate, the darshan pairs both principles simultaneously across institutional spheres: within the ten-member family, goods are shared according to need without weighing individual differences in skill or daily output (AA, pp. 1, 119–120), while between families, villages, and regions, goods exchange at equal labour value evaluated across skill, proficiency, speed, time, and means, free of profit and loss (AA, pp. 66, 76, 119, 145). When a person employs intellect (panditya) to invent an original tool or technique that reduces physical effort, the darshan neither grants a patent monopoly nor relies on individual consumption differentials: the originality is formally recorded in the tradition and honoured with awards (puraskar as righteous wealth, svadhan, AA, pp. 140, 144), while the tool is openly disseminated so that the unit labour value of the product is revised downward and required working hours fall for every family (AA, pp. 56–58, 118, 145). At the same time, the darshan rejects the ground of Marx’s remedy. The hypothesis that everything functions through conflict mistakes existence, in which every unit has inherent strength and progresses through mutual complementarity; class struggle cannot be the foundation of happiness (JV, p. 156). Axiology: Value Theory §3.8 compares the two accounts of labour value in more detail.

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: 4.4 Marginal utility, scarcity, and non-satiation

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: In the 1870s, William Stanley Jevons, Carl Menger, and Léon Walras abandoned the classical labour theory of value. They argued that labour time alone cannot explain why water is more useful than diamonds yet commands a lower price, why labour spent on an unwanted object creates no exchange value, or how heterogeneous capital goods and waiting time enter into prices. In place of labour cost, they grounded exchange value in subjective marginal utility, the additional satisfaction a consumer expects from the last unit of a good (Jevons 1871). Modern economics took its standard definition from this marginalist turn through Lionel Robbins: economics studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses (Robbins 1932; SEP-PE). Scarcity in this sense is relative to wants that are taken as given and, in consumer theory, as non-satiated, so that more of a good is always preferred or at least not refused. Economists commonly present non-satiation as a modelling assumption rather than a claim about human nature, and the theory of choice can be formulated without it. In practice, the assumption that wants exceed means organises the discipline’s central problems: allocation, efficiency, and growth.

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: The darshan answers both sides of this turn. Against a purely mechanical labour theory, it holds that labour creates value only insofar as it establishes genuine usefulness and aesthetic value for assessed human need: the chain runs from labour-based object to object-based usefulness to usefulness-based valuation (AA, p. 49). Against marginalism, it refuses to collapse usefulness into subjective desire or money willingness to pay. Usefulness is an objective relation between the properties of an object and the definite requirements of the body and society, so a kilogram of grain retains the same usefulness whatever its market price (JV, pp. 136–137). Nature is abundant, bodily needs are definite, and scarcity appears where indefinite want, or a deliberate withholding of goods, meets finite means. The darshan names the premise that necessities are infinite and means limited as the very lesson from which people stray into struggle, accumulation, and comfort (§2.3).

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: 4.5 Absolute and relative needs

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: John Maynard Keynes distinguished absolute needs, felt whatever the situation of others, from relative needs, satisfied only if they lift a person above others. The latter, he wrote, may indeed be insatiable, while the former could be met within a century, after which the economic problem might cease to be the permanent problem of humankind (Keynes 1930). Thorstein Veblen had described conspicuous consumption and pecuniary emulation, in which goods serve as marks of standing (Veblen 1899). Fred Hirsch argued that positional goods, whose value depends on others not having them, set social limits to growth that more production cannot overcome (Hirsch 1976).

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: These accounts come nearest to the darshan’s distinction between definite bodily need and indefinite want. They locate insatiability in social comparison. The darshan agrees that comparison of more and less is a form of delusion: the method of relativity keeps widening the distances of big and small, more and less, and a point of contentment is needed that is the same in all humans (AA, p. 60). It traces comparison further back, to a jeevan that has not found its own satisfaction and so measures itself against others.

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
