passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: 4.6 Money, credit, and mutual-credit clearing

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: Most money in modern economies is created by commercial banks when they make loans, rather than lent out from prior deposits, and its quantity is limited mainly by the demand for credit, the banks’ assessment of risk, and monetary policy (BoE 2014). Interest on debt-created money is one of the mechanisms through which ecological economists argue that present economies depend on continued growth (Jackson 2017). Silvio Gesell made the darshan’s contrast between perishable goods and imperishable money the centre of his reform. Because goods decay and money does not, money holders can demand interest as the price of releasing money into circulation; he proposed money that loses value over time, so that it circulates like the goods it represents (Gesell, Natural Economic Order). By contrast, cooperative mutual-credit clearing networks, such as Switzerland’s Wirtschaftsring (WIR), founded in 1934, allow participating producers and households to trade goods and services against book-entry credits and debits on a central ledger without interest-bearing bank loans, expanding trade when cash is scarce (Stodder 2009). The darshan’s critique of symbolic value reaches Gesell’s diagnosis by a different road, and its account of the village exchange-reserve (§3.13) uses ledger clearing of the kind demonstrated by mutual-credit cooperatives to remove the occasion for interest rather than to tax money’s advantage.

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: 4.7 Ecological and post-growth economics

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen argued that the economic process transforms low-entropy matter and energy into high-entropy waste, so that no economy can grow indefinitely on a finite earth (Georgescu-Roegen 1971). Herman Daly proposed a steady-state economy, with constant stocks of people and artefacts maintained by the lowest feasible throughput of matter and energy (Daly 1974). Kate Raworth’s doughnut joins a social foundation of human needs to an ecological ceiling of planetary boundaries (Raworth 2017), and Tim Jackson defines prosperity as the capability to flourish within ecological limits rather than as rising consumption (Jackson 2017). Earth-system scientists now assess six of nine planetary boundaries as transgressed (Richardson et al. 2023). The circular economy, as promoted in industry and policy, seeks to keep materials in use and design waste out of production.

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: These programmes share the darshan’s judgement of unlimited growth and its insistence that production stay within natural balance. Their accounts of why growth continues are institutional: debt, competition, employment, and political pressure. The darshan adds a reason at the level of the person, and its cycle includes the renewal of human capacity and the closure of need, not only the closure of material loops.

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: 4.8 Gandhian economics: permanence and right livelihood

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: J. C. Kumarappa contrasted an economy of transience, which draws down stocks accumulated by nature over ages, with an economy of permanence, which lives within the cycles of nature and recognises the interdependence of all its parts (Kumarappa 1945). He classified economies by their relation to others and to nature, from the parasitic and predatory to those of service, and advocated decentralised village production. E. F. Schumacher’s “Buddhist economics” sought maximum well-being with minimum consumption, treated non-renewable resources as capital to be conserved, and held that work develops human faculties rather than being only a cost (Schumacher 1973). Of all the economic traditions considered here, these are closest to avartansheel arthshastra in content: village autonomy, cyclical energy and agriculture, production by the many, and restraint in wants.

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: 4.9 Needs, capabilities, embeddedness, and institutions

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: Several bodies of work address the questions that cyclical economics must answer in practice. Manfred Max-Neef and his colleagues argued that fundamental human needs are few, finite, and classifiable, and the same across cultures and periods, while the means of satisfying them, the satisfiers, vary (Max-Neef et al. 1989). Len Doyal and Ian Gough grounded universal basic needs in health and autonomy, and distinguished them from wants and preferences (Doyal and Gough 1991). Amartya Sen showed that evaluation cannot rest either on commodity holdings or on subjective utility, which adapts to deprivation and persuasion, and proposed assessing economic arrangements by people’s substantive functionings and capabilities to lead lives they have reason to value (Sen 1999). Karl Polanyi argued that human economies were historically embedded in social relationships, and that treating land (nature), labour (human life activity), and money (a token of purchasing power) as “fictitious commodities” ruled by self-regulating market prices disembeds the economy and corrodes both society and nature (Polanyi 1944). Friedrich Hayek argued that knowledge of particular circumstances is dispersed among many people and that the price system communicates it without any central authority possessing it (Hayek 1945). Elinor Ostrom showed that communities can govern shared resources through polycentric institutions that neither markets nor states supply (Ostrom 2010). Each of these bears on a specific part of the darshan’s proposal: the definiteness of need and capability, the refusal to treat nature, labour, and currency as ordinary commodities, the information that exchange beyond the village requires, and the governance of common natural assets.

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: 4.10 Calculation, planning, and labour accounting

passages.heading: 4-economic-theory-on-wants-scarcity-and-wealth
passages.section: 4. Economic theory on wants, scarcity, and wealth
passages.text: In the debate over economic calculation, Ludwig von Mises and Hayek argued that without market prices a planned economy cannot compare the costs of alternative uses of resources, because the knowledge that prices summarise is dispersed and often tacit. Wassily Leontief’s input–output analysis represents an economy as a table of the inputs each sector requires from every other (Leontief 1936). From such a table the total labour required, directly and indirectly, to produce a unit of any good can be computed. Paul Cockshott and Allin Cottrell argued that modern computing makes economy-wide labour-time accounting feasible, and that labour time can serve as a rational basis for calculation and exchange, with priorities decided democratically (Cockshott and Cottrell 1993; Cottrell and Cockshott 1993). Their proposal remains contested on grounds of information, incentives, and the treatment of skill. It shows nonetheless that valuing goods by the labour they embody can be extended beyond the village with accounting methods that already exist.

passages.heading: 5-indian-and-advaita-teaching-on-desire
passages.section: 5. Indian and Advaita teaching on desire
passages.text: 5. Indian and Advaita teaching on desire

passages.heading: 5-indian-and-advaita-teaching-on-desire
passages.section: 5. Indian and Advaita teaching on desire
passages.text: 5.1 Desire as an unquenchable fire

passages.heading: 5-indian-and-advaita-teaching-on-desire
passages.section: 5. Indian and Advaita teaching on desire
passages.text: The insatiability of desire is a familiar theme in Indian thought. The Bhagavad Gita traces a chain from dwelling on sense objects to attachment, from attachment to desire, from desire to anger, and from anger to delusion and the loss of discrimination (BG 2.62–63). It names desire, born of rajas, as the enemy that covers knowledge, an insatiable fire (BG 3.37–39). The Manusmriti states that desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of its objects, but grows like a fire fed with clarified butter (Manu 2.94). These texts agree with the darshan that enjoyment does not quiet desire and that desire obscures understanding.

passages.heading: 5-indian-and-advaita-teaching-on-desire
passages.section: 5. Indian and Advaita teaching on desire
passages.text: 5.2 The fullness of the Self and the place of wealth

passages.heading: 5-indian-and-advaita-teaching-on-desire
passages.section: 5. Indian and Advaita teaching on desire
passages.text: Advaita Vedanta explains desire by ignorance of the Self. The Self is complete, and things are dear for the sake of the Self rather than for their own sake; desire arises when the Self is mistaken for the body and mind, so that a limited being seeks completion in objects (Axiology: Value Theory §§2.1–2.4; BU 2.4.5). The remedy is knowledge of the Self, prepared by disciplined action without attachment to its fruits (BG 3.19). Wealth, artha, is a legitimate aim of life when pursued within dharma, but liberation stands above it, and the renunciate’s path leaves economic life behind (Axiology: Value Theory §§2.2, 2.4–2.5).

passages.heading: 5-indian-and-advaita-teaching-on-desire
passages.section: 5. Indian and Advaita teaching on desire
passages.text: The structural parallel with the darshan is clear. In both, insatiability arises from mistaking one’s being for the body and seeking in objects a fulfilment that objects cannot give. The darshan locates the remedy in understanding jeevan and coexistence, which is directed into family, production, and exchange, while Advaita locates it in knowledge of a Self for which the world of exchange has only empirical reality.

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: 6.1 Homeostatic satiety

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: Physiology confirms that the body regulates its own intake. The central nervous system integrates signals from fat stores and the gut, among them leptin, insulin, and ghrelin, to match food intake to energy expenditure and to keep body weight within a range over long periods (Morton et al. 2006). Bodily need has a definite measure, and the body has mechanisms that recognise when it has been met.

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: 6.2 Wanting, liking, and hedonic hunger

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: The same research distinguishes this homeostatic regulation from motivation that runs beyond need. Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson separate “wanting”, the incentive salience mediated largely by dopamine systems, from “liking”, the hedonic impact of a reward. The two can come apart: wanting can be sensitised and grow while liking does not, which helps explain compulsive pursuit of rewards that no longer satisfy (Berridge and Robinson 2016). Michael Lowe and Meghan Butryn describe “hedonic hunger”, appetite driven by the anticipated pleasure of food in the absence of any energy deficit, as distinct from homeostatic hunger (Lowe and Butryn 2007). These findings give an empirical counterpart to the darshan’s distinction between definite bodily need and the inexhaustible cycle of selection and taste.

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: 6.3 Adaptation and the income–well-being debate

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: People adapt to many changes in circumstance, though less completely than the original “hedonic treadmill” theory supposed. Set points are not neutral, differ among individuals, and can change (Diener et al. 2006). Richard Easterlin found that richer people within a country report greater happiness, while average happiness did not rise as national income grew over time (Easterlin 1974). Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton found that life evaluation rises with the logarithm of income while day-to-day emotional well-being levelled off at moderate incomes (Kahneman and Deaton 2010). Later work found no plateau on average, and a joint reanalysis located the plateau among the least happy minority (Killingsworth 2021; Killingsworth et al. 2023). Axiology: Value Theory §4.3 discusses this evidence. The data support neither a simple satiation point for income nor its absence. They show that more income does not close the gap between life evaluation and lived experience for many people, which is consistent with, though it does not establish, the darshan’s claim that material means cannot meet the need being placed on them.

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: 6.4 Earth-system limits

passages.heading: 6-the-sciences-of-satiation-and-natural-limits
passages.section: 6. The sciences of satiation and natural limits
passages.text: The biogeochemical cycles that sustain life, of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and water, have been altered by human activity on a scale that now pushes several of them beyond the conditions of the past ten thousand years (Richardson et al. 2023). Thermodynamics sets a further limit on every production process (Georgescu-Roegen 1971). The darshan’s claim that extraction disturbs the earth’s balance and that production must keep to the proportions of natural regeneration is, in its general form, consistent with this science. Several of its specific causal hypotheses, such as the possible effects of extraction on the earth’s magnetic current or of cosmic rays on the stability of water (AA, pp. 31, 80–82), are not supported by current earth science and are treated as open in §9.7.

passages.heading: 7-comparison
passages.text: 7. Comparison

passages.heading: 7-comparison
passages.text: 7.1 Where insatiability comes from

passages.heading: 7-comparison
passages.text: The traditions disagree most sharply on the source of insatiable want. Neoclassical theory takes non-satiation as given and does not ask its source. Aristotle and Marx locate limitlessness in the pursuit of money as such. Veblen, Keynes, and Hirsch locate it in social comparison and positional goods, while Sen, Max-Neef, and Doyal and Gough separate objective human needs and capabilities from subjective utility and market preferences. The Gita and Advaita locate insatiability in desire arising from ignorance of the Self. The sciences describe mechanisms, sensitised wanting, hedonic hunger, and adaptation, without a theory of what the person is seeking. The darshan places the source in the joint form: a jeevan whose higher activities lack understanding, whose discontent is read as a shortage of objects, and whose inexhaustible capacity for selection and taste is left without regulation. On this account the other explanations describe real consequences of the same error.

passages.heading: 7-comparison
passages.text: 7.2 What counts as wealth, and what closes the cycle

passages.heading: 7-comparison
passages.text: For the money economy, wealth is measured in currency and its growth is the aim. For classical and Marxian economics, wealth is the product of labour, but capital accumulates in money. For ecological economics, wealth must stay within throughput limits, and the circular economy closes material loops. For Polanyi, treating land, labour, and money as market commodities disembeds the economy from society. For the darshan, economics has no standing in isolation from the five dimensions of human orderliness; wealth is only the produced object; money is a symbol; and the cycle closes in three places together: need is definite, goods are used rather than hoarded, and natural assets are used in proportion to their regeneration. The circular economy addresses the third. Daly’s steady state addresses the second and third. Only the darshan, Gandhian economics, and in part Keynes make the first, the definiteness of need, a condition of the economy’s structure.

passages.heading: 7-comparison
passages.text: The traditions also value labour, skill, and invention differently. Since the marginalist revolution, market economics has priced goods by subjective marginal utility, treated labour as a factor of production paid the price it commands (Jevons 1871), and rewarded technical invention through temporary monopoly rents and patents. Marx grounded the value of commodities in socially necessary labour time, reduced skilled labour to multiplied simple labour by the training embodied in the worker (Capital I, ch. 1), and separated post-capitalist distribution into a first stage of labour-time certificates, which he acknowledged still apply an unequal standard to individuals of differing talent and family dependency, and a later stage of distribution according to need (Marx, Gotha Programme). Labour-time accounting likewise computes values from the average hours and inputs embodied in goods (§4.10). The darshan holds that labour is a joint exertion of mind (manas) and body that creates value because it establishes objective usefulness and beauty for assessed need (AA, pp. 49, 143). Rather than deferring need-based sharing to a distant stage or rewarding invention through monopoly pricing, it pairs four mechanisms simultaneously across institutions: inside the ten-member family, goods are shared according to need without weighing individual labour or dependency ratios (AA, pp. 1, 119–120); between families, villages, and regions, the labour value of goods is determined by the total combination of skill, proficiency, speed of work, time, and means alongside scholarliness, honoured according to capacity, ability, and receptivity, and exchanged free of profit and loss (AA, pp. 119, 145; §§3.6, 3.12); original tools, procedures, methods, and formulas are formally recorded and honoured with social prizes (puraskar) as righteous wealth (svadhan) (AA, pp. 140, 144); and once disseminated through education and the ten-tier council network, improved tools lower the unit labour value of goods so that across society the means of production increase and the time required decreases (AA, pp. 56–58, 118, 145; §3.9).

passages.text: 7.3 Summary of the positions

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: The darshan joins two kinds of order in one sequence. Knowledge is law, law is regulation, and regulation is balance; balanced living is justice in humans; living within universal orderliness with justice is dharma, that is, resolution; and realisation in coexistence is dharma and truth (MVD, p. 173). Law (niyam), regulation (niyantran), and balance (santulan) are already evident in the orders other than the human, which are bound by their own laws (AA, p. 117). Justice (nyaya), dharma, and truth (satya) are the evaluations by which humans establish their own orderliness, and they are the activities the treatise describes as still under review in human tradition (AA, p. 18).

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: This distinction sets the division of labour for any instrument used in a cyclical economy. Where a relation is governed by law, regulation, or balance, and can be stated as a quantity, a rate, a constraint, or a rule, it can be measured, recorded, modelled, and in part handled by an instrument: the regeneration rate of a forest, the fertility of a field, the stock in a store, the labour time and means embodied in a product, the balance of an account, or the matching of regional surpluses and deficits. Where a question concerns the fulfilment of a relationship, the purpose of a choice, or its accord with coexistence, it belongs to human evaluation.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: The darshan also states how instruments should be trusted. Every instrument is conceived, planned, and produced by human beings, and their mentality is embodied in its planning. An instrument falls short of the purpose for which it was planned, so trust in it and use of it should stay below that purpose, and every signal it gives must still be read by a human being (KD, p. 139). Technique multiplies the speed of whatever it serves, problems included (SB, p. 267). Artificial Intelligence and Coexistence §§1.2–1.5 places present AI systems in the material order as insentient instruments, yantra, that can reproduce the outward pattern of evaluation by pleasure, bodily advantage, and gain and so amplify delusion, or, directed by explicit humane criteria, make the basis of a decision visible to the people who make it.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents

passages.text: 8.2 Why databases and network connectivity alone are not enough

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: Writing in the 1990s, Shri A. Nagraj anticipated the role of computing in a self-governing economy. The treatise prescribes a detailed household and village survey before self-governance begins (AA, pp. 122–125), sets measurable criteria for evaluating each of the five committees across ten tiers (AA, pp. 146–149), expects computers to be used in the village exchange-reserve (AA, p. 138), and envisages every committee linked by a computer network from the village to the world, so that information located anywhere is accessible to the village (AA, p. 132).

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: A closer look at what the cyclical economy and the ten-tier self-governing order require shows why passive databases and network connectivity, while necessary, cannot by themselves establish this system or enable a rapid transition from the present economy. A database stores tables of records, and a network transmits them from one terminal to another. Neither can interpret unstructured local reality, compute dynamic multi-tier balances, or help individuals and committees interpret what the records mean at the moment of action. Four structural bottlenecks explain why intelligent systems and AI agents are needed as core infrastructure components rather than mere ledgers.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: The part-time governance and producer-staffing constraint. In the treatise’s institutional design, self-governance is not run by a class of full-time officials. Members of the village council and its five committees are part-time representatives who continue their own physical production in their families (AA, p. 127). The village exchange-reserve, which handles storage, valuation, and clearing for a hundred families, is staffed by as few as three people (AA, p. 138), and across society at least eighty percent of people remain prosperous in production while at most twenty percent serve in coordination (MVD, p. 259). If ten tiers of five committees had to manually enter and query database tables, reconcile seasonal surpluses and deficits across thousands of villages, trace multi-stage labour values, and audit ecological regeneration, governance would either stall under cognitive and administrative overload or require a large full-time bureaucracy. Creating such a managerial class would reproduce the shift from a working mindset to a managing mindset that the darshan identifies as an obstacle to universal participation in production (JVD, p. 35; AA, p. 107).

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: The non-price coordination and calculation bottleneck. In a market economy, prices and interest rates compress dispersed local information about supply, demand, and scarcity into a single number that anyone can read, though they distort value through speculation, unequal purchasing power, and profit-seeking (§4.9; Hayek 1945). Replacing market prices with raw database records across millions of goods, variable seasonal yields, tool and building depreciation, and Ricardian differences in soil and mineral fertility (§§4.2, 4.10; Ricardo 1817; Leontief 1936) creates an immense coordination task. Passive databases do not propagate a local harvest shortfall through an inter-regional input–output matrix, separate natural endowment from human effort, or generate feasible options for routing surpluses to cover deficits (AA, p. 72) and scheduling multi-year infrastructure without interest rates. Without intelligent systems that continuously compute these relationships and present plain options to human councils, non-price coordination cannot scale beyond a handful of villages.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: The qualitative-to-quantitative translation bottleneck. The treatise’s instruments of self-governance combine numerical stocks with qualitative local judgements: a family’s assessment of its common and special aspirations (AA, pp. 26, 112), the village survey of skills, land, water, and cottage industries (AA, pp. 122–125), the joint planning of multi-occupation training by the education, production, and exchange-reserve committees (AA, p. 131), and the periodic evaluation of all five committees (AA, pp. 146–149). Traditional database software demands rigid forms and technical query languages that turn producers into clerks. Intelligent agents can converse with ordinary producers and family representatives in natural language, structure qualitative observations into living records, cross-check them against settled rules of law, regulation, and balance, and translate multi-tier accounts back into clear, local summaries.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: The transition bottleneck before universal awakening. The cyclical economy cannot wait until every participant is already fully awakened (anubhav-moolak). It must be built and operated during the transition by people who are moving toward awakening (anubhav-gami) while still living inside a surrounding currency and market economy. During this transition, individuals still carry conditioned habits of evaluating by pleasure, bodily advantage, and gain (priya–hita–labha; JV, pp. 72–73); families are still learning to distinguish definite bodily and social need from sensory or positional want (§2.3); and village exchange-reserves must navigate the treatise’s three stages of exchange (AA, pp. 142–143), maintaining dual ledgers in wholesale currency prices and midpoint labour values while protecting the village against outside speculative arbitrage (AA, pp. 136–138). A passive database records a drift into overconsumption, hoarding, or unequal exchange only after the damage is done. Active intelligent agents can provide reflective feedback to individuals and families before choices harden into habit, and can handle the dual-ledger complexity that would otherwise overwhelm early transitional communities.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: 8.3 AI agents across the ten-tier order: from the individual and family to the world council

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: The companion technical note on a personal AI assistant argues that while today’s commercial AI systems act as amplified four-and-a-half-activity machines tuned to capture attention and stimulate appetite, a personal AI assistant designed under the darshan’s criteria can serve an individual in transition (anubhav-gami) as a diagnostic mirror, an educational companion, and a practical assistant, helping the person recognise delusion in real time and act toward awakening. Establishing and governing a cyclical economy requires extending that principle from the individual to every human unit in the ten-tier family-rooted self-governing order (parivar-mulak swarajya vyavastha). In this architecture, each human unit, from the person and the family to each committee and council across all ten tiers, works together with a corresponding AI agent whose scope matches the unit’s responsibilities.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: The individual and the Personal AI Assistant. Paired with the individual producer and learner, the personal AI assistant supports the transition from restricted (priya–hita–labha) evaluation to humane conduct (Technical Note: The Personal AI Assistant §§2–3). As a diagnostic mirror, it helps the person notice when consumption, work, or interpersonal choices are driven by sensory impulse (ruchimulak), status comparison, or the urge to take more and give less, prompting reflection against justice, dharma, and truth. As an educational companion, it supports sustained study (adhyayan) of coexistence alongside practical learning across multiple occupations, such as agriculture, dairy, cottage crafts, and machine repair, so the individual becomes self-reliant in occupation and free of occupational fear (AA, pp. 64–65, 131). As a practical assistant, it logs the person’s work pace, time, and skill development for the producer’s own review and, where the producer chooses, for village labour accounting.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: The family and the Family AI Agent. In Madhyasth Darshan, the family of ten to twelve members, not the isolated individual, is the primary unit of society and the site where need is assessed, prosperity is evidenced, and goods are shared according to need without weighing individual labour (AA, pp. 9, 14, 26, 65, 119–120). A Family AI Agent, governed by the family and its chosen representative (mukhiya), supports the household as a collective unit:

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: Assessing definite need and tracking right use: It helps the family formulate and periodically review its annual and seasonal requirement for common aspirations (food, shelter, adornment, and health and education equipment) and special aspirations (telephony, broadcasting, and transport; AA, p. 112). By comparing actual household consumption and stock age against assessed need, it gives the family early warning when goods are sitting idle, spoiling, or drifting into comfort-seeking accumulation (JV, p. 152; AA, p. 75), or when a member’s health or educational need is going unmet.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: Coordinating family production and restfulness: It helps the household coordinate daily and seasonal work across agriculture, kitchen, care, and family industry so that work remains restful (vishram) rather than exhausting (KD, pp. 12–13; AA, p. 24), while keeping internal family distribution completely free of individual labour-time accounting (AA, pp. 119–120).

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: Interfacing with the village while preserving household privacy: Rather than exposing internal household conversations to higher tiers, the Family AI Agent publishes only the structured summaries the village requires: the family’s assessed seasonal needs, planned production, expected surplus for the exchange-reserve, and available skills.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: The family cluster, the village council, and the five Committee AI Agents. At the first two tiers of self-governance, ten families form a family cluster (tier 1) and ten clusters form a village of roughly a hundred families (tier 2) with a village family council and five functional committees: education-sanskar, health-restraint, justice-security, production-work, and exchange-reserve (AA, pp. 14–15, 125–145). Pairing an institutional AI agent with the family cluster and with each of the five committees turns the village survey (AA, pp. 122–125) into a continuous, self-updating operational picture and links the five dimensions horizontally:

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: The Production-Work Agent aggregates family production plans across the nine branches of village production (agriculture, go-shala, forestry, cottage industry, and related crafts; AA, pp. 133–136), tracks soil fertility, water tables, and forest regeneration against extraction (AA, pp. 142, 146), and computes local labour paces and input requirements.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: The Exchange-Reserve Agent works alongside the three-person exchange-reserve staff (AA, p. 138) to manage inventory, monitor stock age against spoilage, maintain family accounts, and run the dual currency-and-labour-value ledgers required during the three stages of transition (AA, pp. 136–138, 142–143).

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: The Education-Sanskar Agent receives projected skill-gap signals from the production and exchange-reserve agents and helps the education committee schedule multi-occupation training so that every villager develops competence across multiple trades (AA, p. 131).

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: The Health-Restraint Agent links household nutritional and medicinal requirements with the production committee’s crop and medicinal-plant plans and monitors village sanitation and occupational health indicators (AA, p. 139).

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: The Justice-Security Agent monitors whether exchange ratios, resource extraction, and household security indicators remain within the bounds of the four dimensions of justice (evaluative, behavioural, production, and exchange justice; AA, pp. 141–143) and prepares factual records when the committee is called to resolve a dispute or review an exception.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: Tier 3 to Tier 10 Council and Committee AI Agents. From the ten-village council (tier 3) and hundred-village council (tier 4) up to the world family council (tier 10; AA, pp. 27–30, 115, 126–127), institutional AI agents paired with each tier’s council and five committees communicate through an open, federated protocol. Instead of centralising raw household data in a single state mainframe, each tier’s agents exchange aggregated surplus-and-deficit vectors, inter-regional input–output coefficients, labour-value distributions, and watershed or biome regeneration metrics with adjacent tiers. This agent-to-agent network performs three tasks that make rapid transition and large-scale coordination feasible:

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: Multi-tier supply, demand, and scale matching: Agents identify where one village or district has a surplus of grain, cloth, or timber and another has a deficit, routing exchange at equal labour value without speculative middlemen (AA, p. 72). They also coordinate inputs and outputs across the treatise’s division of industrial scale: cottage industry in the village, small and medium industry at intermediate tiers, and large industry at higher tiers for transport, telecommunications, and heavy machinery (AA, pp. 29–30, 115).

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: Guided transition management: When a new cluster of families or villages enters the first stage of transition, its local agents immediately connect to existing regional exchange-reserve agents, inheriting calibrated labour-value benchmarks, dual-pricing calculators, and mutual-credit clearing links so the community does not have to invent its accounting infrastructure from scratch.

passages.heading: 8-bringing-the-economy-into-balance-measurement-intelligent-systems-and-multi-level-ai-agents
passages.section: 8. Bringing the economy into balance: measurement, intelligent systems, and multi-level AI agents
passages.text: Keeping governance participatory and part-time: Because the agents continuously perform the data collection, cross-committee synchronisation, input–output calculation, and constraint checking, the part-time human representatives at every tier (AA, p. 127) can review clear options, verify the underlying evidence, and devote their deliberative time to the human judgements of justice, dharma, and truth.

Within the multi-level architecture of §8.3, the agents at the family, village, and regional tiers watch these indicators continuously and route early warnings to the responsible human unit. The table pairs each condition with what can be recorded, the early signal of failure, and the question that the signal returns to people.
